groups.why: Both describe the defeat of Azcapotzalco and formation of the alliance; s2 identifies the three former vassals.
Together they establish that 'Azteca' is a modern label that the Triple Alliance Mexica did not use for themselves.
The Codex Osuna's alternate term is an example of the broader point that Nahuatl had no single exclusive name for the alliance.
Chinampas are the example of the advanced agricultural techniques said to support prosperity.
These identify cacao and copper-alloy axe pieces as objects used as currency; the specific cacao crisis and axe form add detail.
Both describe cacao's use as currency, with s35 specifying its role in small daily purchases.
Both describe the blending of Nahua religious inheritance with other traditions, and s47 names the two traditions.
Both explain human sacrifice as feeding the sun and describe the ritual's victims and purpose.
Both state that the Mexica imposed a commercial blockade on Tlaxcala; s54 gives its duration.
Both describe the agreement that preserved Tlaxcala's independence in exchange for participation in the flower wars.
The account of the Taximaroa campaign supplies the event behind the claim that it was the sole Mexica military attempt in Michoacán.
Both list the regions over which the Mexica and their allies extended their rule.
Both describe the three-city alliance; s108 also gives its origins and relative strengths.
Both state that Tenochtitlan became the alliance's leading city and de facto imperial center.
Both describe the huey tlahtoani as the chief ruler; s118 specifies the offices and authorities held.
Both describe the judicial system's courts and jurisdiction, with s123 detailing its hierarchy.
